new_statements.quote: One [Torricelli; Sandaun, PNG] regularly assigns stress to the penultimate syllable, but verbs allow for stress on either syllable of the final foot, resulting in contrasts such as [ˈte.re] ‘chop’ and [te.ˈre] ‘howl’. While forms like the noun [ˈte.li] ‘round thing’ would be equally legitimate for a verb, *[te.ˈli] with final stress is not a possible noun.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable by default; in verbs only, stress may fall on either the penult or the final syllable of the final foot (a lexical penult/final contrast confined to verbs), whereas nouns are categorically penultimate. Offered as an example of stress placement 'sensitive to morphosyntactic factors', weight-insensitive.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs may carry final stress (lexical contrast [ˈte.re] 'chop' vs [te.ˈre] 'howl'); nouns never do. Nothing on words longer than two syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, isolated word forms (no citation-form/phrase discussion). On the identity of the variety: the source says 'One' generically with no citation; Donohue's One = the Molmo variety (Donohue 2000 fn.1), i.e. Molmo One [aun] molm1235, a sister lect of Southern One under Glottolog's six-way split. Southern One is never named; the only Southern One-specific first-hand data (Donohue & Crowther 2005, 'Siama' variety) say the One varieties have no tone (p.181, Table 4) but nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's Southern One [osu] (sout2932) corresponds to Crowther 2001's southern One villages Siama, Wondu, Foluapu and Alkula (Glottolog ref 77430 language code; Laycock 1973 lists Alkula and Siama under ONE). Ethnologue's osu entry instead lists Karantu, Koiniri, Parara, Romei and Wolwale (population 200), villages that Crowther/Glottolog and SIL's Onnele materials assign to Northern One [onr] (nort2907), so the two catalogues' 'Southern One' do not coincide. The quoted stress statement is about generic 'One' = Donohue's Molmo One [aun] (molm1235), not Southern One; the only Southern One-specific data (Donohue & Crowther 2005, Siama variety) concern segments and the absence of tone.

sources.citation: Donohue, Mark & Melissa Crowther. 2005. Meeting in the middle: interaction in North-Central New Guinea. In A. Pawley, R. Attenborough, J. Golson & R. Hide (eds), Papuan Pasts (Pacific Linguistics 572), 167-184. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics.
sources.note: The only first-hand Southern One data found: the 'Siama' One variety (= Southern One [osu] per Glottolog ref 77430 language code) appears in the north-south comparison pp.178-179 (wordlist items, *s loss, *t>r absent in Siama, *l>n in Siama), in the consonant/vowel inventory Tables 2-3 (Siama: p t k m n f s w l y; i e ɛ a o u), and p.181: 'Tonal systems are consistently absent in the Torricelli languages (relevant here are the One varieties)'; Table 4 (p.182) Siama row has no pitch contrasts. No statement about stress placement anywhere in the chapter.

tone.quote: Tonal systems are consistently absent in the Torricelli languages (relevant here are the One varieties), and the western languages (Sentani, Tobati, Ningera). The tonal systems in the phonologies of the Skou family languages are completely dominant, and remarkably comparable (Donohue 2003). Tonality in the Serra Hills languages varies inversely with their distance from the Skou languages, suggesting that tone is an areal phenomenon supported by the simple syllable-based tone systems of the Skou languages.
tone.locator: p. 181 (prose below Table 3); Table 4 'Comparative suprasegmental inventories', p. 182, rows One: Siama / Inebu / Romei with empty 'Pitches' cells
